items.label: f01-durable-before-visible
items.front: Order of operations for a crash-safe local JSON commit?
items.back: Write a temp file, fsync, close, renameSync over the data file, and only then publish the new state in memory. A lock file opened with 'wx' is the writer lease (EEXIST becomes 503, never waited on or stolen).

items.label: f03-uncertain-vs-conflict
items.front: How does an uncertain response differ from a 409 conflict, and how does the UI handle it?
items.back: A conflict means the server refused; an uncertain response (network failure) means it may already have committed. The UI marks the write uncertain and blocks further saves until the user reviews the latest state, because without receipts a retried POST could create a second record.

items.label: f02-global-key-oracle
items.front: Flag keys are unique across all projects and the 409 says 'Flag key "X" already exists'. Risk and fix?
items.back: It is an oracle revealing other projects' keys to anyone who can create flags. Decide key scope explicitly: per-project keys (audit every key-only lookup) or global keys with a generic message.

items.label: f04-authorize-first
items.front: Rule for ordering validation that reads stored data against authorization?
items.back: Authorize first. Validation messages derived from a stored record describe it to whoever asked; run requireProjectWrite before validateStrategySettings (and validateVariant), keeping only the low-risk 404 on random ids ahead of the 403.

items.prompt: A constraint is rewritten as plan not_in [free]. A context arrives with no plan field. What does the constraint evaluate to, and why?

choices.text: false: a missing context value never matches, even through not_in or inversion
true: an absent plan is not 'free', so the not_in [free] constraint is satisfied
error: the evaluation throws and the whole request fails with a 500
true: but only when the constraint also has inversion turned on

items.explanation: evaluation.js returns false when the raw value is not scalar, before any operator logic; removing that line would let every plan-less context through to the rollout check.

items.prompt: Why would answering evaluate requests with 304 Not Modified keyed on the snapshot ETag be a bug?

choices.text: It is not a bug; flag decisions are identical for all users who evaluate against one snapshot
The snapshot cache evicts entries quickly; 304 answers would be unreliable under heavy load
The ETag names the configuration, not the caller; one snapshot gives different users different answers
ETags change on every request; a 304 keyed on them would never be returned to any client

items.prompt: Why does #commit publish the new state in memory only after renameSync succeeds?

choices.text: renameSync is asynchronous, so the new state has to wait for it to resolve first
renameSync deletes the lease file, so publishing earlier would release the lock
The in-memory cache is cleared during the write, so there is nothing to publish
Otherwise readers could see a change that a later disk failure rolled back

renameSync deletes the lease file, so publishing earlier would release the lock

items.explanation: The file is written, fsynced and renamed into place, then #accept publishes the exact bytes; the guide calls durability and visibility separate events.

items.prompt: bucketValue maps users to 1..100 and a rollout matches when bucket <= rollout. Why is the range 1..100 rather than 0..99?

choices.text: So rollout 1 enables nobody and rollout 99 everybody
So the hash prefix never has to be reduced modulo 100
So rollout 0 enables nobody and rollout 100 everybody
So that a missing userId can be assigned bucket 0

choices: So rollout 1 enables nobody and rollout 99 everybody
So the hash prefix never has to be reduced modulo 100
So rollout 0 enables nobody and rollout 100 everybody
So that a missing userId can be assigned bucket 0

items.explanation: (numeric % range) + 1 shifts the range; a boundary test built on bucketValue itself catches the off-by-one that 200 random users rarely hit.

items.prompt: Two sibling variants each have weight 60. Why can no single-field validator reject that, and what inconsistency does the codebase have here?

choices.text: Each 60 is valid alone; only the sum breaks the rule, and it answers 422 in the contract but 400 or 409 in the service
A weight of 60 is out of the allowed range; the contract and the service both reject it with 422
Weights are checked only in the browser; the server accepts any sum and answers 200 to both layers
The sum is enforced at evaluation time; the weights are silently normalized to 50 each and saved

items.explanation: Cross-field invariants need a set-level check; the review (R3) recommends standardizing semantic failures on 422 so clients can tell a conflict from a malformed request.

items.prompt: A project_member of the Checkout project holds a token with the write scope and tries to edit a flag in a different project. What happens?

choices.text: 200: a write-scoped token may edit the flags of a project it is not a member of
403: the write scope is not enough without a membership row for that project
401: the token is refused as it was issued while working in the Checkout project
404: flags in another project are hidden from users who are not an admin

choices: 200: a write-scoped token may edit the flags of a project it is not a member of
403: the write scope is not enough without a membership row for that project
401: the token is refused as it was issued while working in the Checkout project
404: flags in another project are hidden from users who are not an admin

items.explanation: Effective permission is the intersection of token scope, instance role and per-project membership; only instance_admin skips the membership check.

items.prompt: An editor loaded revision 8 and saves with If-Match: "8", but another user committed revision 9 in between. Why are the service's permission checks still safe even though they are check-then-act?

choices.text: The writer lease blocks other reads while an editor has a form open, so the second commit cannot start
Checks use the request's frozen snapshot, and the commit is refused (409) if version or digest changed
They are not safe, and the second write silently overwrites revision 9 without raising a conflict
Checks re-run after the write succeeds, and the write is reverted if any of them fails on the new state

items.explanation: Under #withLease the store compares meta.version and the digest with what the request expected; any mismatch throws 'State changed; reload and review before saving'.

So variant choice is independent of rollout position
So a user's variant changes on every request, for fairness
So variants can be stored per user, like rollout buckets
